claims.claim: Religion and culture are interwoven: cultural traditions may emerge from religious traditions, and may influence them.
Culture has material and nonmaterial elements, and values, beliefs, symbols, and language are elements of culture; religious teachings can shape the values a society holds in high regard.
Religious traditions shape cultural domains including art and music, architecture (houses of worship), food practices (fasts, feasts, dietary rules), calendars and festivals, and language.
Culture shapes religion through language and translation: translating scripture involves deliberate choices of wording that affect how teachings are understood in new contexts.

Regional customs blend with traditions, so the same tradition can be expressed very differently across regions; people of the same branch of a religion may celebrate holidays very differently based on where they live.

The boundary between religious and cultural practice is contested: festivals, clothing, and food are cases where participants and scholars debate whether a practice should be classified as religious, cultural, or both.
Clifford Geertz described religion as a cultural system: a system of symbols tied to conceptions of a general order of existence, combining a worldview and an ethos.

Popular culture is the pattern of cultural experiences and attitudes found in mainstream society, often spread through commercial media; religious stories, symbols, and imagery circulate there, and communities respond in varied ways.
The material culture of religion includes buildings, ritual objects, and dress, whose forms carry meaning and change over time and across cultures.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a practice such as a festival, an item of clothing, or a food should be classified as religious or cultural.
positions: Some participants and observers emphasize the religious meaning of a practice and treat it primarily as religious.
Others emphasize its cultural, national, or family meaning and treat it primarily as cultural.
Many hold that the practice is both at once and that no single label fits it.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the boundary as contested and context-dependent: it describes participants' varied understandings and the scholarly debate rather than declaring a single correct classification.

sourceRecords.title: 3.1 What Is Culture? — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER source, read live 2026-08-21. Supports: culture as material (tangible objects such as buildings, clothing, and ritual items) and nonmaterial (ideas, attitudes, beliefs); material and nonmaterial aspects as linked, with physical objects symbolizing cultural ideas; cultural universals such as funeral rites, weddings, and celebrations of births, and language. Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 3.2 Elements of Culture — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER source, read live 2026-08-21. Supports: values as ideals, principles, and standards members of a culture hold in high regard; beliefs as tenets or convictions people hold to be true; the significance of symbols and language to a culture. Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 3.3 Pop Culture, Subculture, and Cultural Change — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A OER source. The live 3e page requires JavaScript for automated fetch, so the identical section was read live on the 2026-08-21 on the Introduction to Sociology 2e edition page (https://openstax.org/books/introduction-sociology-2e/pages/3-3-pop-culture-subculture-and-cultural-change); the canonical 3e URL is registered. Supports: popular culture as the pattern of cultural experiences and attitudes that exist in mainstream society, often expressed and spread via commercial media such as radio, television, movies, and the music industry; subcultures as smaller cultural groups within a larger culture. Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 15.2 World Religions — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry record reused with identical URL; read live 2026-08-21. Supports the lesson's core framing: the observation that cultural traditions may emerge from religious traditions or may influence them; the point that people from the same branch of a religion may celebrate holidays very differently based on where they live; religious traditions as differing in organization, belief, history, and use of sacred texts and objects. Facts synthesized; no source prose adapted.
